items.t: His website goes live: the desk and the lens
items.s: On 24 November 2026 his website, tmadealex.github.io, went live, redesigned as "the desk and the lens": every page is seen through one of two pieces of glass, his trading screen or his camera. Night and morning looks, PARTY_MODE, a cursor that leaves little candles, a trading desk that straightens as it comes up, and an iris, a film roll and a contact sheet for his photography. It sets no cookies, has no forms and no tracking, and asks search engines not to list it.

items.t: His home on GitHub is set up: nine repositories, five public and four private
items.s: On 23 November 2026 a member of his community set up a home for TMade Alex on GitHub, the TMadeAlex organisation, as a gift. It has nine repositories (a repository is one folder of work with its full history): five public, including his website, and four private. Everything was built and checked on one computer first, and went up on GitHub on 24 November. TMade Alex decides what stays.

items.s: Why the source behind these pages stays private, and how only the finished pages are ever published.
items.x: TL;DR: Everything you're reading is written in a private repository. An automated job builds the site, sends only the finished pages to a public repository, and reads every one of them first. If anything in them is something no machine or person has read, the publish stops. How it works, step by step Two repositories, one direction There are two repositories behind these pages: 1. changelog astro (private): the entries, the drafts, the write ups and the site's code. 2. changelog astro public (public): only the finished pages, which GitHub Pages serves. Nothing ever flows from public back to private, and nobody edits the public one by hand. What happens on every update When an entry is saved
